name: Reassurance seeking (rate me threads)
lead: A rate-me thread is a forum post in which a user shares photos and asks other members to rate or critique their face and features. On looksmaxxing forums such as looksmax.org, these threads are used to get a read on where someone stands and which features (skin, jaw, hair, body fat, posture) might be improved, so the poster can choose what to work on next.

Responses typically include a numeric score, comments on specific features, and a short list of suggestions. One looksmax.org reply to a teenage poster, for example, simply listed sport, diet, chin exercises and temporalis training as the route to improvement [2]. Many threads follow a title-and-age format with a tag such as "be brutal" requesting blunt feedback [3][4].

In clinical psychology, repeatedly asking others to confirm how one looks is called reassurance seeking and is described as one of the repetitive behaviors in body dysmorphic disorder, alongside mirror checking, comparing and camouflaging [1]. Research on appearance-related social comparison and on feedback seeking in social media exists, but no published study has examined rate-me threads themselves [5][6].

angle.text: People post to learn how their features read to others and to collect specific suggestions, such as skin care, leanness, hair or grooming changes. The feedback is then used to prioritize a looks-improvement plan.

paras: A poster uploads front and side photos, often with age and height in the title, and asks for a rating. Replies commonly give a score on an informal scale and name features that hold the face back or stand out [2][3][4]. Some posters ask for "brutal" honesty or for advice on how to "ascend" [3][7].
Threads are usually short. Many receive a one-line rating and a suggestion; others attract extended feature-by-feature breakdowns.

Wikipedia describes reassurance seeking as a common behavior in body dysmorphic disorder, together with mirror checking, comparing and camouflaging. It also notes that heavy selfie-taking and social media use are linked to low self-esteem and body dysmorphic tendencies, with users sometimes seeking validation through likes and comments, and that a 2020 systematic review found appearance-focused social media use linked to body image dissatisfaction [1].

Related research examines appearance-related social comparison as a possible mechanism behind appearance-related psychopathology [5], and associations between social-media feedback seeking, popularity and depressive symptoms in adolescents [6]. Studies of reassurance seeking in obsessive-compulsive disorder compare it with compulsive checking [8]. These studies cover broader behaviors, not rate-me threads specifically.

Rate-me threads are a staple of looksmaxxing forums and are the usual first post from new members. Posters say they use the ratings to benchmark themselves and choose interventions; some threads include before-and-after follow-ups showing the effect of changes in grooming or fitness [2][3].

No studies found on rate-me threads. Cognitive-behavioral therapy for body dysmorphic disorder, which includes exposure and response prevention aimed at rituals such as reassurance seeking, has been tested in randomized trials [1].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, rate-me threads are treated as a routine way to get feedback and a starting list of features to improve.

claims.claim: Ratings from other members show what to improve
claims.believers: Posters ask for "brutal" feedback and advice on how to ascend, and repliers answer with feature-specific plans such as training, diet and chin exercises [2][7].
claims.experts: No published study has tested the accuracy or usefulness of forum ratings. Clinical literature describes repeated appearance reassurance seeking as a behavior associated with body dysmorphic disorder [1].

card.note: Little published research on rate-me threads themselves.

quick.overview:
Rate-me threads are forum posts where people share photos and ask for ratings or critiques of their looks.

Clinically, frequent reassurance seeking about appearance is described as a behavior in body dysmorphic disorder.
quick.mechanism: Users post photos and receive ratings or feedback from other members.
quick.risks: No studies specific to these threads were found; related research links appearance-focused social media use to body dissatisfaction.
